### INSTRUCTIONS FOR GEMINI 4 ARGON:
You are acting as an independent **Managing Director and Senior Forensic Technology & IT Services Financial Auditor**. 
You have been provided with the complete, chronological working paper compiled during a section-by-section forensic capture of iOCO Limited's financial disclosures (37 total sections across primary report and companion disclosures).

Notice how this working paper is constructed:
1. At each stage, specific text, accounting notes, APMs, and operational tables were extracted directly from the report.
2. Across the sections, an **Open Questions Ledger** evolved dynamically: anomalies and high-level management claims in early sections were flagged with priority levels, specific verification instructions, and carried forward as `Pending` until verified against primary financial statements, detailed accounting notes, and subsequent continuous disclosures.
3. **Crucial Post-Year-End SENS Updates:** Material disclosures (Part 2) released subsequent to the financial year-end provide decisive evidence resolving or altering key pending questions from the Annual Report (e.g. debt facility execution/drawdown, cash runway, project development milestones, and operational permits).

**YOUR MANDATE:**
Review the sequential evidence trail below. Trace how the questions evolved from initial anomalies to audited reconciliation. **Do not produce a forward equity research forecast or valuation report.** Your role is **forensic reasoning only**: you must evaluate the working papers and independently reach your own definitive determinations on the core accounting, operational, and balance sheet junctions, explicitly factoring in subsequent SENS disclosures.

---

## REQUIRED STRUCTURE OF YOUR AUDIT REPORT

Please format your response into the following four clear sections:
1. **Executive Forensic Audit Summary:** Concise synthesis of the group's true economic performance, balance sheet health, post-balance-sheet liquidity runway, and key findings.
2. **Detailed Forensic Reasoning & Determinations:** Step-by-step walkthrough of each key technology junction (contract revenue mix across recurring ARR/managed services vs lumpy system integration/hardware resale, gross profit margin by line of business, direct technical headcount utilization and labor costs, contract assets / WIP unbilled revenue and deferred revenue recognition, capitalized software development & IP amortization, legacy dispute / litigation provisions & contingent liabilities, debt restructuring / deleveraging milestones, and FCFE conversion), citing specific notes, tables, and calculations.
3. **Audit of Common Surface-Reading Pitfalls:** Contrast your findings against the common errors made by naive readers.
4. **Final Forensic Verification Matrix:** A clean markdown summary table listing each Junction, the Raw Initial Claim, the Resolving Note/SENS Announcement, and your Final Verified Determination.

Many people picture a CEO in a corner office 
issuing decrees like a warlord in the middle of 
a coup. 
Nothing could be further from the truth. In 
short, Ashona, as the Group CFO, plays a 
key role in keeping the head office running 
optimally, along with 13 business unit 
executives striving to deliver to shareholders a 
more consistent operational performance. 
Yet, if I was an outside shareholder, I would 
want more granularity. So here goes. 
Diversity sits at the heart of iOCO. Our 4 000 
people are diverse, our businesses are diverse 
and our customers are diverse. We often hear 
that diversity is a strength. In 2026, this proved 
true. When one business felt pressure from 
changes in technology and customer spending, 
another picked up the baton and ran hard to 
make up the shortfall. Overall, the result was 
adequate: revenue grew 3% to R5.733 billion 
(yes, we can, must and will do better), adjusted 
EBITDA was R624 million (2025: R516 million) 
and earnings rose 38.7% to R357 million. 
HOW DO YOU RUN A BUSINESS 
AS DIVERSE AS iOCO?
When we restructured iOCO in 2025, it 
became clear that a group this diverse could 
not be run from the centre. A huge expensive 
head office was not the answer. However 
large the CEO’s office, no one person in it 
can keep a finger on the pulse of call centres 
in Randburg, an IT services operation for a 
pharmaceutical company in Switzerland and 
an AI project in Saudi Arabia. The history of 
EOH and iOCO bears this out: the old EOH 
performed best when a small head office 
gave the operating businesses a degree of 
autonomy. We went further in 2025, adopting 
a more decentralised structure that we call 
“radical autonomy”. 
Initially, I got it wrong. 
Last year’s annual report shows four business 
units, each meant to operate autonomously, 
with a Business Unit Chief Executive (BUCE) 
running it as though it were their own. Those 
four units were largely a product of EOH’s 
history: some had previously lost divisions 
through disposals, and some had managers 
who were poorly placed to execute the 
strategy. Most importantly, having only four 
units stifled the talent one layer down. During 
2026, we took a hard look at each unit, asked 
what made sense operationally rather than 
historically, and pushed radical autonomy even 
further by increasing the number of business 
units from four to 12

--- Section D003 | [AR] physical page 13 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
The result has been good. Most encouraging 
has been the energy and drive of the new BU 
MDs now running their own businesses. After 
all, it is the talent of these BU MDs that will 
determine iOCO’s long-term success. 
Compared with a year ago, I am more 
confident that we now have the managers 
in place to deliver growth. There will be 
more changes as we refine the model, as 
smaller businesses grow in importance and as 
acquisitions bring in the talent we need to give 
our customers a complete service. 
These 13 business unit (BU) MDs, together 
with our CFO, Ashona, and me, form iOCO’s 
Executive Committee (EXCO). Combined, 
the EXCO has over 170 years of technology 
experience. This brings a wide mix of skills 
while maintaining a small, focused head office. 
AUTONOMY WITH 
ACCOUNTABILITY
Autonomy needs accountability. In effect, 
when we “anoint” a BU MD, we are handing 
him or her the keys to their own kingdom. 
That is a big leap to make without some 
oversight. Some of these are large businesses, 
with revenue close to R1 billion and EBITDA 
of over R100 million. On their own, some of 
these business units would be worth over 
R1 billion.
INCENTIVES
Each business unit agrees a budget, and 
incentives are paid only if it is achieved. In 
FY2026, the incentives were based mostly on 
revenue and EBITDA. For 2027, changes were 
necessary. Our working capital management fell 
short of our expectations (do not worry, we 
have worked hard to fix this since year end). 
To plug the hole, 30% of the incentive is now 
based on achieving a 45-day working capital 
cycle. We have also increased the number 
of employees incentivised on our long-term 
share price performance. While we love 
radical autonomy, there is value in encouraging 
collaboration across businesses, and a shared 
interest in the share price does that. 
Financial controls
Part of Ashona’s role (a small part) is to ensure 
tight financial accountability. Many of the 
business units can be working-capital hungry 
(hence the change to incentives above), and 
without a tight rein this can be the Achilles 
heel of any services business. Think about 
this – if we extend terms of 60 or 90 days to 
a customer, iOCO has to fund three months 
of salaries (by far our biggest cost) which 
are a non-negotiable payment that cannot 
be delayed. If late payment follows, you can 
understand how quickly a services business can 
unravel. Each business unit’s Financial Director 
reports into Ashona’s central finance team. 
Streamlining risk approval
Our history requires a rigorous review of 
tenders and large contracts. This year, we 
reviewed the framework for approval by a 
Risk Committee. The process was historically 
cumbersome, with too many voices offering 
opinions and risk not managed effectively. 
Interestingly, this opportunity made its way to 
shareholders who approached me to outline a 
plan to streamline this process. This is positive 
shareholder interaction as we rethought our 
approach and have adopted a more dynamic 
approach.
Our new approach has three decision-makers 
(so there is never a tie): the BU MD, Ashona 
and me. Since introducing this streamlined 
process, we are managing risk better and 
reaching more balanced decisions. 
MONDAY MORNINGS
When I became involved with iOCO, we 
instituted a weekly meeting at 10am on 
Monday. Over time these meetings have 
improved. Each business unit head presents an 
update answering two simple questions: what 
happened last week, and what is planned for 
the week ahead? We hold the meeting on a 
Monday to stimulate thinking on a Sunday. 
Each business also has its financial performance 
reviewed against budget, forward load and the 
prior year. Importantly, the BU MDs present 
to the full EXCO, so they are accountable not 
only to the CEO and CFO but also to each 
other. The meetings also spark discussion on 
cross-selling opportunities and on working 
more seamlessly with customers. This year, 
we introduced a leaderboard. Each month the 
leaderboard is published ranking the BU MDs 
on revenue and EBITDA growth against the 
prior year and budget. 
Radical autonomy is being embedded in the 
core of how iOCO is run. Besides fostering an 
owner-manager mindset and peer competition, 

--- Section D003 | [AR] physical page 13 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
the model allows iOCO to scale. It sets 
iOCO up to be a much bigger business than 
it is today without incurring the cost of more 
central overheads. 
A LOOK BACK AT iOCO’S 
HISTORY
From its listing on the JSE in 1998 until 
2016, iOCO, then known as EOH, was one 
of the best-performing companies on the 
exchange. Over that period, revenue grew 
at a compound annual rate of 40%, EBITDA 
at 37% and the share price at 30.3%. The 
main reason for EOH’s success was a series 
of acquisitions, coupled with some organic 
growth. Acquisitions accounted for two-thirds 
of the growth. 
Yet EOH made “only” 15 material acquisitions 
between 2000 and 2016, about one a year. 
Together, these acquisitions produced a 25% 
return on investment. The market rewarded 
EOH for this acquisition-led earnings model. In 
short, EOH allocated capital well.
Here is the interesting part. Our 2026 results 
sit between EOH’s 2013 and 2014 results: 
similar profits, but a very different valuation. 
iOCO’s market capitalisation today is 
R2.4 billion. EOHs was R7.9 billion at the end 
of 2013 and R14 billion by 2014.

--- Section D003 | [AR] physical page 14 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
I can add the most value to shareholders 
helping close this gap.
My main job, therefore, is to make iOCO a 
trusted, capable serial acquirer again, and to 
keep it that way for many years, until we get 
back to being a trusted capital allocator. 
Here is how we are going about it.
THE SERIAL ACQUIRER 
MACHINE
Each year, iOCO generates over R624 million 
of EBITDA. Some of the cash goes to taxes 
and interest, but most is available for two uses: 
reinvesting in iOCO to make it stronger and 
more resilient, and returning excess capital to 
shareholders. 
REINVESTING TO MAKE iOCO 
A STRONGER, MORE RESILIENT 
BUSINESS
A “known known” of operating in the 
technology sector is that change comes at 
you rapidly and inevitably. While technology 
businesses do not have high capex or 
depreciation, they must keep reinvesting to 
remain relevant. And as technology evolves, 
gaps appear in the product suite. Filling those 
gaps keeps iOCO in the game. Instead of 
capex, investment is framed as acquisitions. 
Our BU MDs know their businesses best; after 
all, they run them. Each is encouraged and 
incentivised to find acquisitions that fill gaps in 
the products or services they offer. They have 
embraced the idea. 
After some brief engagement with a potential 
target, an idea becomes an opportunity and 
passes to the finance team, which conducts 
due diligence and works out how to structure 
the transaction for the best return at the 
lowest risk. For example, decisions need to 
be made on whether to use our R1.1 billion 
of assessed tax losses, whether to mitigate 
risk through profit warranties, and where the 
acquisition should sit within iOCO (normally 
under the BU that brought in the idea). Once 
that work is done and we have a price range, 
we weigh each opportunity against three 
criteria: 
1.	 Other acquisitions being evaluated in the 
Group
2.	 Our internal hurdle rate, a return of more 
than 20%
3.	 The valuation that iOCO trades at on 
the JSE. 
So far, we have made two acquisitions, and a 
third is under discussion. Ashona’s CFO report 
sets out the criteria for companies we want to 
acquire. Perhaps what we are after is captured 
by a dialogue I had recently.
Earlier this year, we met the founder and 
management team of a potential acquisition. 
During our meeting, I asked the founder if he 
was married. 
His response? “I have been married since 
1980.” 

--- Section D003 | [AR] physical page 14 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
I asked him to score his love for his wife out of 
10, with 10 being the highest. 
His answer? 9.5. 
I then asked him to score his love for the 
Company he founded out of 10. 
His answer? 11.
Those are the businesses, and the managers, 
we want to join iOCO. Generally, these are 
small businesses with a concentrated customer 
base. Because iOCO has more than 3 000 
customer relationships, doors open once they 
are inside the iOCO tent, and they can pursue 
far wider opportunities. We also leave these 
companies alone, applying radical autonomy to 
them just as we do to our existing businesses. 
iOCO is a great home for a loved business. 
SHAREHOLDER RETURNS
The other use of the capital generated in 
through share buybacks. This is only an option 
when we assess iOCO to be undervalued in 
the equity market. The benefit of continuously 
evaluating other companies for acquisition, 
is that it gives us a very good idea of market

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

D003 contains **no footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references)** in the supplied evidence. However, several embedded qualifications and small-print-style admissions carry material forecasting implications:

- **"Our working capital management fell short of our expectations (do not worry, we have worked hard to fix this since year end)"** [D003, p. 13]. This is the single most consequential qualification in the section. It is a direct admission that FY2026 working capital was worse than planned, and that remediation occurred **after** year-end (i.e., FY2027). This must be tested against: (a) the cash conversion ratio (Q101/Q79); (b) contract assets/WIP and receivables aging (Q32/Q85); (c) the 45-day working capital cycle incentive target for FY2027 — which implies the FY2026 actual cycle was **above 45 days**. **Verification needed**: what was the actual FY2026 working capital cycle in days? This is a new question for D004.

- **"Some of these are large businesses, with revenue close to R1 billion and EBITDA of over R100 million. On their own, some of these business units would be worth over R1 billion."** [D003, p. 13]. This is an unquantified sum-of-the-parts claim. It implies at least one BU has ~R1bn revenue and >R100m EBITDA (i.e., >10% EBITDA margin at BU level). **Verification needed**: which BU, and does the segmental disclosure (D005–D016) support a >10% EBITDA margin at that scale? This feeds directly into the Q75 International GM collapse question — if a large BU is performing well, the drag must be concentrated elsewhere.

- **"Our 2026 results sit between EOH's 2013 and 2014 results: similar profits, but a very different valuation. iOCO's market capitalisation today is R2.4 billion. EOHs was R7.9 billion at the end of 2013 and R14 billion by 2014."** [D003, p. 13, table]. The comparison table (Revenue R5,733m vs R5,086m/R7,220m; Operating profit R483m vs R495m/R719m; Profit R357m vs R331m/R492m; Market cap R2,400m vs R7,900m/R14,000m) is a **valuation argument, not a financial disclosure**. It confirms FY2026 operating profit R483m and profit R357m (consistent with D006/D007). **Caution**: the table is unaudited narrative context — do not use as a forecast input beyond confirming the headline figures already captured.

- **"decisions need to be made on whether to use our R1.1 billion of assessed tax losses"** [D003, p. 14]. This is a material tax disclosure buried in narrative. It implies **R1.1bn of assessed tax losses** available to shelter future acquisition profits. This directly bears on Q33/Q87 (DTA recoverability R130,366k, unrecognised DTAs, tax loss carry-forwards). **Verification needed**: reconcile R1.1bn assessed tax losses to Note 9 unrecognised DTA and Note 27 tax reconciliation. If R1.1bn is genuinely available, the effective tax rate on future acquisitions could be materially below 27%.

- **"Our internal hurdle rate, a return of more than 20%"** [D003, p. 14]. This is the stated acquisition hurdle rate. Relevant to Q2/Q17/Q18 (goodwill impairment, CGU WACC) — if the hurdle rate is >20% return, the implied discount rate used in impairment testing should be consistent. **Verification needed**: compare Note 7 CGU discount rate to the stated >20% hurdle.

- **"Generally, these are small businesses with a concentrated customer base."** [D003, p. 14]. This is a risk qualification on the acquisition strategy — acquired targets have customer concentration. Relevant to Q37 (top-10 customer concentration) and Q32/Q85 (ECL on concentrated debtors). **Verification needed**: post-acquisition, does group customer concentration increase?

- **"we have made two acquisitions, and a third is under discussion"** [D003, p. 14]. Confirms two acquisitions completed in FY2026 (consistent with MySky, Q8/Q59/Q84/Q96) and a third in pipeline. **Verification needed**: identify the second acquisition (MySky is one) — is it disclosed in Note 14? This is a new question for D010.

- **"4 382 employees"** [D003, p. 14] vs **"Our 4 000 people"** [D003, p. 12]. Minor internal inconsistency in headcount rounding (4,000 vs 4,382). Relevant to Q70 (employee costs R2,236,516k, headcount, average cost). **Verification needed**: confirm actual FY2026 headcount in D004/D010 employee benefit note.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references) are present in the supplied D004 evidence (pp. 15–18).** The section is narrative CFO commentary with two area-captured highlight/infographic blocks. However, several **embedded qualifications and definitional ambiguities** require unpacking:

1. **"Revenue increased by 3% to R5.73 billion on a constant currency basis"** [D004, p. 16] vs highlight table "Revenue R5 753 million +3% (constant currency)" [D004, p. 15].
   - **Tension**: The highlight table shows **R5,753 million**, but the audited/segment revenue per D009 is **R5,732,561k** (Q46, resolved). The **R20.4m difference** is unexplained. The "+3% constant currency" qualifier means the **reported (nominal) growth rate is not stated** — reported revenue grew only R149,341k (+2.7%) per Q15. This is a **definitional qualification**: constant-currency growth overstates nominal growth. Must verify in D010 (Note 22 revenue disaggregation) whether R5,753m is a rounded/restated figure or a different revenue definition (e.g., including discontinued operations or gross vs net).

2. **"Recurring revenue exceeding 60% during FY2026"** [D004, p. 16].
   - **Qualification**: "Exceeding 60%" is a **threshold claim, not a precise figure**. No definition of "recurring" is given (does it include software support/SLA maintenance, managed services, cloud hosting, SaaS — or also multi-year project annuities?). This directly feeds **Q37/Q77/Q83** (Note 22 IFRS 15 disaggregation). Must verify the exact recurring % and its composition in Note 22.

3. **"Adjusted EBITDA grew by 21% to R624 million"** [D004, p. 16] and "Operating profit increased by 15% to R483 million" [D004, p. 16].
   - **Qualification**: "Adjusted EBITDA" is a **non-IFRS measure** — the R624m figure implies adjustments of **R141m above operating profit** (R624m − R483m), which must include D&A (~R108m per Q67) plus the **R13,479k non-recurring legacy items (Q69)** plus other adjustments. The **composition of the R141m bridge is not disclosed here** — must verify in D009/D010 (Note 24 / adjusted EBITDA reconciliation). Critically, if R13,479k "non-recurring" items are added back but restructuring is ongoing (Q102), adjusted EBITDA is **overstated on a sustainable basis**.

4. **"Bank debt, excluding IFRS 16 lease liabilities, reduced to R480 million as of 31 July 2026"** [D004, p. 18].
   - **Qualification**: This is **bank debt only, excluding leases**. Gross debt per Q29/Q60 is **R619,337k** (which includes lease liabilities). The **R480m bank debt vs R619,337k gross debt implies ~R139m of lease/other liabilities** — must reconcile to Note 18 (Q29/Q60/Q92). Also, "reduced to" implies a prior-year comparison that is **not stated** — must obtain FY2025 bank debt to compute the reduction quantum.

5. **"Net finance costs reduced by 32% year-on-year"** [D004, p. 18].
   - **Qualification**: No absolute net finance cost figure is given. Per Q41, finance costs were **R67,724k**; a 32% reduction implies prior-year net finance costs of ~R99.6m (if FY2026 net finance cost ≈R67.7m less investment income R7.1m ≈R60.6m; 60.6/0.68 ≈R89m prior year — arithmetic needs verification). Must reconcile to Note 26 (Q41/Q63).

6. **Capital allocation infographic: "+R80m organic, +R90m inorganic, +R100m balance sheet, +R70m buybacks"** [D004, p. 17].
   - **Qualification**: These are **allocations, not cash flows**. The R70m buyback allocation vs **R68,836k actual repurchases (Q49)** is broadly consistent (R1.2m gap). The **R90m M&A allocation vs Note 14 acquisition cash flows (Q59: net cash inflow +R7,914k)** appears contradictory — if R90m was deployed on M&A, why was there a net cash *inflow* from acquisitions? Must verify in Note 14 (Q59/Q110). The **R100m "balance sheet resilience"** is not a cash flow line and its meaning is unclear — must clarify.

7. **"New multi-year wins R2.1 billion"** [D004, p. 15–16].
   - **Qualification**: This is a **contract-win TCV (total contract value) metric, not revenue**. It is not comparable to annual revenue (R5.73bn) and says nothing about **when** revenue is recognized or **margin**. Must verify whether any portion is already in contract liabilities/deferred revenue (Note 22) and the **average contract duration** to annualize.

8. **"Return on equity 35%"** [D004, p. 15–16].
   - **Qualification**: No definition given (profit after tax ÷ average or closing equity?). Per Q45, equity is roughly R1.0bn (profit R351,010k ÷ 35% ≈ R1.0bn). Must verify the equity denominator in the AFS.

BUILDING A RELIABLE UTILITY BASELINE
Managing utilities across a large property portfolio requires more than consolidating bills. 
Consumption, tariffs, meter information and billing quality need to be understood at site level 
before performance can be reliably monitored.
During the first phase of the programme, APhinity consolidated and validated utility information 
across 104 sites, covering 2 284 bills and approximately R212.1 million in electricity and 
water spend in FY2026.
The resulting bill-by-bill baseline provides a foundation against which new utility information can 
be tested, while highlighting data gaps and areas requiring further investigation.
The source identifies 68 sites in the higher data-quality bands as assurance-ready, with the 
remaining 36 requiring further data fixes.
The assurance model tests new bills against the established baseline and tracks findings through 
defined stages, separating opportunities under investigation from outcomes that have been 
confirmed. 

--- Section D005 | [AR] physical page 41 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
STRENGTHENING ENVIRONMENTAL DATA
The process is also improving visibility of the consumption data required for environmental 
reporting. Of the first 104 sites assessed, 76 had readable electricity consumption data, 
while 28 still required meter readings or other data before Scope 2 emissions could be 
calculated from their utility bills. 
Better utility data creates the foundation for stronger financial control, environmental 
measurement and ongoing resource management

--- Section D005 | [AR] physical page 42 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
IDENTIFYING VALUE AT RISK
Analysis of the initial portfolio identified an estimated R8.46 million savings opportunity 
pipeline. The opportunities span tariff and demand adjustments, energy efficiency, water leaks 
and historical claims. 

--- Section D005 | [AR] physical page 42 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
CONNECTING COST AND ENVIRONMENTAL PERFORMANCE
The baseline is also providing greater visibility of the portfolio’s environmental profile. For 
sites with sufficient underlying data, the analysis annualised 32.2 million kWh of grid electricity 
consumption, corresponding to approximately 29 168 tCO2
e of Scope 2 emissions. It also identified 
approximately 2.76 million kWh of annual solar generation across 23 sites, representing 7.9% of 
electricity within the relevant analysis

--- Section D005 | [AR] physical page 42 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
BUILDING FROM THE FIRST 104 SITES
The first phase establishes the data and assurance foundation for a broader portfolio approach. 
At the date of the submitted project update, approximately 250 additional sites were scheduled 
for baselining, with the intention of progressively extending monthly assurance across the wider 
property portfolio.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Critical finding — footnote definitions are MISSING from this capture.**

- **Page 39 table** contains numerous footnote markers embedded in the "MARKET OPPORTUNITY," "INDUSTRIES," "PEOPLE," and "PARTNERS AND IP" columns: `[^Hi][^gh]`, `[^Me][^dL][^ow]`, `[^Si][^xt][^ar][^ge][^te][^d]`, `[^Hu][^aw][^ei]`, `[^Or][^ac][^le]` `[D005, physical PDF p. 39]`. **The corresponding footnote definitions are NOT present in the supplied evidence.** These markers appear to be an artefact of the PDF text-extraction layer (likely highlighting/annotation tags rather than true financial footnotes), but this cannot be confirmed. **Do not infer their content.** A verification question is raised below.

- **Page 40 "KEY HIGHLIGHTS"** contains a similar marker cluster: `[^sa][^le][^sc][^ap][^ab][^il][^it][^yt][^hr][^ou][^gh]` (appears to spell "sales capability through") and `[^re][^po][^si][^ti][^on][^in][^gf][^ro][^ma]` (appears to spell "repositioning from") `[D005, p. 40]`. These are almost certainly **text-extraction artefacts of highlighted/annotated words**, not financial footnotes — but the definitions are absent and must not be reconstructed. Flag for confirmation.

- **"the margin caveat"** appears as a standalone fragment in the page 39 table (bottom-right region) `[D005, p. 39]`. This is a **qualification fragment whose full sentence is cut off by the capture boundary** (capture warning on p. 40 notes "boundary crosses text"). The phrase signals management is explicitly caveating margins — consistent with the "Hyperscaler commoditisation compressing infrastructure margins" risk on p. 40. **The full caveat text is missing** and must be retrieved.

- **"Commenced repositioning from a traditional infrastructure-led business into an outcome-led cloud, AI and managed services provider"** `[D005, p. 40]` — a forward-looking qualification implying the FY2026 revenue base is still substantially legacy infrastructure-led (lower-margin resale/consumption), with the higher-margin managed-services mix only building. This is a **mix-shift timing risk** for FY2027 forecasting: do not assume immediate margin uplift.

- **"Cloud SA enters FY2027 as a standalone division"** `[D005, p. 40]` — structural change. Implies Cloud SA was previously reported within a larger cluster (likely Infrastructure Solutions or iOCO Enterprise). This affects **segment comparability and restatement** (links to Q73 restatement disclosure). Must confirm how Cloud SA was reported in FY2025/FY2026 segment tables.

- **Energy-as-a-Service (EaaS)** — "proof of concept completed in FY2026 and scheduled for launch in Q1 FY2027" `[D005, p. 40]`. New revenue line with **no FY2026 revenue**; any FY2027 EaaS revenue in the forecast is speculative and should be modelled as upside only.

- **APhinity utility programme** `[D005, p. 41–42]` — this appears to be a **client case study** (a property-portfolio utility management engagement), not Cloud SA's own financials. The R212.1m electricity/water spend, R8.46m savings pipeline, 104 sites, 32.2m kWh, 29,168 tCO2e are **client metrics**, not iOCO revenue. **Do not mistake these for Cloud SA financial inputs.** Flag as a potential misread risk.

under full production loads to determine the realised gains.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote markers present but definitions MISSING from this capture:**
- Page 43 table contains footnote markers `[^Hi][^gh]`, `[^Me][^dL][^ow]` in the "MARKET OPPORTUNITY" column header area [D006, p. 43]. **The corresponding footnote text is NOT present in the supplied evidence.** These markers appear adjacent to "Large, mature market; infrastructure demand is cyclical" and "Opportunity lies within the AI and data platform and hybrid cloud environments." The definitions may clarify market-sizing methodology, AI/data platform scope, or hybrid cloud definitions. **Verification question raised (see Q141 below).**
- Page 43 contains two visible asterisk footnotes:
  - `* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology` — attached to "R400 billion* +2%*" [D006, p. 43]. This qualifies the **R400bn SA IT services market size and +2% growth** as **management's own methodology**, not an independent source. Forecast implication: the +2% market growth is a management assertion; the 13% CAGR for managed security is similarly unverified.
  - `* Management ambition` — attached to "Grow market share to 2% over 36 months" [D006, p. 43]. This is an **aspiration, not guidance**. No revenue bridge is provided to quantify what 2% market share equates to in Rand terms.

**Qualification on performance claims (p. 45):**
- "Vendor-documented performance characteristics indicate an anticipated 35–40% reduction in latency and 2× throughput... **These figures represent design expectations rather than realised client performance.** Once the refreshed environment is deployed, aggregate production usage will enable actual performance to be measured and validated against these expectations" [D006, p. 45]. This is an explicit **forward-looking qualification** — the case study describes a design-stage project, not a delivered outcome. No revenue or margin contribution is quantified.
- "Deployment of the new systems has been **rescheduled** while the trading-platform provider completes certification of a new operating system" [D006, p. 45]. This is a **project delay disclosure** — revenue recognition on this refresh project may slip into FY2027. No quantum disclosed.

**Qualification on recurring revenue (p. 43):**
- "10% of revenue recurring" [D006, p. 43] — this is a **very low recurring mix** for an IT services division. Combined with "90% Managed services and resource augmentation" and "58% Infrastructure solutions" in the "How we earn" box, there is an apparent **internal inconsistency**: if 90% is managed services/resource augmentation (typically recurring), how is only 10% of revenue recurring? This suggests the "10% recurring" may refer to a narrower definition (e.g., multi-year contracted recurring only, excluding time-and-materials resource augmentation). **Verification question raised (see Q142 below).**

**Qualification on market share ambition (p. 43):**
- "Grow market share to 2% over 36 months" — no baseline market share is stated. If SA IT services market is R400bn and iOCO Infrastructure Solutions targets 2%, that implies ~R8bn revenue ambition, which is **larger than the entire group's R5.7bn revenue**. This is either a market-sizing definition issue or an aspirational stretch. **Verification question raised (see Q143 below).**

In October 2025, a multi-site organisation wanted a clearer view of workforce wellbeing, 
organisational culture, trust in leadership and employee engagement across Gauteng, the Western

pressures or the experiences influencing how employees felt about their workplace. The challenge 
was therefore not simply to ask employees what they thought, but to identify patterns in employee 
experience early enough for leadership to respond.
HOW AUTHENTIQ WORKS
The solution combines employee responses with Layered Voice Analysis (LVA) and emotional 
trend analytics. This generates aggregated indicators that help identify patterns of stress, unease, 
trust concerns and wellbeing risk across the organisation and its regions. 
WHAT AUTHENTIQ DOES

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote markers `[^Hi][^gh] [^Me][^dL][^ow]` on "MARKET OPPORTUNITY"** `[D007, p. 47]`: **Footnote definitions are MISSING from this section capture.** The markers recur identically to D006 p. 43 (Q141). They appear attached to market-sizing language ("MARKET SERVED R12 billion* 7%*", "SA fraud-detection spend, growing to R33 billion by 2030", "Alternative legal services ~R2.1 billion", "Long-term insurance premiums ~R615 billion"). The asterisked qualifications that ARE printed are: "* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology" and "* Management ambition" `[D007, p. 47]`. These asterisk notes qualify the R12bn market-served and 7% market-share figures as **management-defined, not independently sourced** — a material caveat for any market-share-based forecast. The bracketed `[^Hi]` etc. remain undefined; must be located in D010 or by re-capture.

- **Market-sizing qualification** `[D007, p. 47]`: "MARKET SERVED R12 billion* 7%*" with "* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology" and "* Management ambition." This means the 7% market-share figure is a **management ambition, not an achieved share**, and the R12bn market-served is **internally sized**. Do not treat as external TAM. Sources cited for sub-markets: "Markets and Markets, TransUnion" `[D007, p. 47]` — but the R12bn aggregate is iOCO's own methodology.

- **Recurring revenue definition qualification** `[D007, p. 47]`: "Recurring and licensing revenue represented 60% of FY2026 revenue; contracted recurring services and licensing represented 85% of the FY2027 opening revenue base." This is a **two-metric disclosure** — 60% actual FY2026 vs 85% "opening revenue base" FY2027. The 85% is a forward-looking contracted-base metric, not an achieved FY2026 figure. Forecast must not conflate the two. Also note "licensing" is bundled into "recurring" — licensing may be perpetual/one-off and inflate the recurring claim; verify in Note 22.

- **Renewal rate inconsistency** `[D007, p. 47 vs p. 48]`: p. 47 states "Renewal rate 97%"; p. 48 states "renewal rate 95%." **Internal inconsistency of 2 percentage points** within the same division section. Flag for verification.

- **"Contracted recurring services and licensing represented 85% of the FY2027 opening revenue base"** `[D007, p. 47]`: This is a **forward contracted-base claim** — implies high FY2027 revenue visibility but is not audited revenue. Verify against Note 22 contract liabilities / backlog (Q122).

- **"Prevented payout of R250 million of fraudulent life and funeral assurance claims"** and **"preventing R40 million in non-compliance penalties"** `[D007, p. 48]`: These are **client value metrics, NOT iOCO revenue**. Must not be mistaken for iOCO financials. Confirm in Note 22 that these are not revenue lines.

- **"Processed 200 000 payroll transactions per month calculated with 99.9% accuracy"** `[D007, p. 48]`: Operational volume metric, not revenue. Note the p. 47 header says "200 000+ pay slips a month" and "3.5 million verifications a year" — operational KPIs only.

- **"Court transcription: AI speech-to-text; further provinces and SADC — Three provinces expanding to nine in FY2027"** `[D007, p. 48]`: Forward-looking capacity expansion claim. Verify FY2027 revenue timing and any capex/AI investment in Note 39 / Note 6.

- **"AI-supported IP: Veritas self-service launched; VeriSENSE and AuthentIQ launched in GRaCE in AWS; ... in development"** `[D007, p. 48]`: Multiple platform launches — check capitalization of development costs (IAS 38) in Note 6 / Note 2.5 (Q95/Q134).

- **"International: AuthentIQ in UK risk environment; further markets Kenya, Namibia, and US in being assessed"** `[D007, p. 48]`: Forward expansion intent — no FY2026 international revenue disclosed for this division. Relevant to Q100/Q104/Q126 (international reconciliation) but no quantification.

- **"attrition 2% per annum"** `[D007, p. 48]`: Very low attrition claim for scarce-skill staff — verify against employee-cost note and retention/SBP provisioning (Q50/Q82).

- **"30 specialists at XTND and 50 in OneSymplexity and 24 in Inlexso"** `[D007, p. 47]`: Sums to 104 — matches "104 critical and scarce skills" in the PEOPLE line. Internal consistency check passes (30+50+24 = 104). Good.

- **"422 billable staff include 104 critical and scarce skills, 243 skilled permanent and fixed-term contracted staff, and 125 semi-skilled administrators, analysts and support staff. 16 non-billable staff."** `[D007, p. 47]`: 104 + 243 + 125 = 472, but billable is stated as 422. **Arithmetic tension: 472 ≠ 422 (difference 50).** Also 422 billable + 16 non-billable = 438 total, which matches "PEOPLE 438." So the 104/243/125 breakdown sums to 472, not 422 — a **R50 head discrepancy** in the sub-category split. Flag as verification question.

Between June 2025 and June 2026, the LD Group enrolled 3 037 learners across four regions, combining 
accredited learning with disability-inclusive support and live learner tracking.
MAKING STRUCTURED LEARNING MORE INCLUSIVE
The LD Group, an iOCO business, delivers accredited learning across Business Analysis, IT Quality 
Assurance and Software Testing, Management and Leadership, Business Administration and entry￾level IT programmes.
Its delivery model combines recruitment and placement, accredited learning and learner support. 
For learners with disabilities, an occupational therapist conducts a functional assessment before 
placement and prepares a Reasonable Accommodation report to guide the support required in 
the classroom and workplace.
INCLUSION DESIGNED INTO DELIVERY
Across three recently closed flagship projects, 36.5% of learners placed were persons with 
disabilities. Of these learners, 57 were female and 44 male. Every learner with a disability 
received an occupational therapist assessment before placement, supported by workplace 

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 59 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
TRACKING THE LEARNING JOURNEY
Every learner is tracked through the LD Group’s eBrixx™ learner management system from 
enrolment to certification. This creates a live record of learner progress and provides funding clients 
with an auditable account of what was completed, rather than only what was attended.
REGIONAL PERFORMANCE
Region Learners Completed Completion rate*
Cape Town 225 74 78.7%

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 59 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
BUILDING PATHWAYS BEYOND COMPLETION
Qualifications are aligned to areas including IT, business administration, management and 
leadership, with entry-level IT programmes designed for new workplace entrants.
FROM PARTICIPATION TO EVIDENCE
eBrixx™ provides a learner record from enrolment through completion, allowing the LD Group 
to evidence participation, learner support and completion across its programmes and regions. 
1 862 learners successfully completed their qualifications.

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 60 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
BRINGING FRAGMENTED WORKFORCE PROCESSES TOGETHER
A financial services client was managing Human Capital activities across separate systems and 
processes, with an affiliate business unable to access several internal systems. The absence of a 
common portal made it more difficult to manage employee information and day-to-day Human 
Capital processes consistently across business units.
Rosstone implemented a cloud-based Human Capital Management platform to consolidate these 
functions into a single environment and provide a central repository for employee information.
ENABLING MORE DIRECT ACCESS TO HUMAN CAPITAL SERVICES
Through a single portal, employees and managers can access self-service functionality alongside 
onboarding, induction and training processes. The platform also provides visibility over employment 
history, benefits and other employee information.
Centralising these functions creates a more consistent route to Human Capital services across 
participating business units while reducing reliance on separate administrative processes

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 61 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
SCALING PEOPLE ALONGSIDE THE BUSINESS
A growing retail client needed to expand its workforce across multiple stores while addressing 
recruitment delays, turnover and inconsistent attendance.
iOCO introduced an integrated workforce model combining a centralised talent pool, recruitment 
tracking, community-based recruitment and workforce management technology. ERS Biometrics 
was integrated with VIP Payroll to strengthen attendance management and payroll administration.
STRENGTHENING WORKFORCE EFFICIENCY AND STABILITY
The centralised talent pool reduced recruitment turnaround to 48 hours, alongside a 
25% reduction in recruitment time and 15% reduction in recruitment costs. Attendance 
reached 98.2%, supporting more consistent staffing across the store network.
A provident fund was introduced for the clients permanent employees to support 
longer-term employee benefits and workforce stability, while consistent candidate communication 
and feedback strengthened the recruitment experience.
The workforce ultimately grew by 100% to 324 on a baseline of 162 client employees across 
11 stores, providing the people capacity required to support the retailer’s expansion

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 61 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
SCALING THE WORKFORCE AS THE BUSINESS GROWS
By combining faster recruitment, workforce technology, employee benefits and community-based 
sourcing, the model supported the retailer’s expansion, while strengthening the systems and talent 
pipeline needed to sustain its growth

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 62 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
MAKING CUSTOMER SUPPORT AVAILABLE AT SCALE
A global consumer electronics company required a multilingual, always-on service and technical 
support capability for consumer, retail and business customers across South Africa and neighbouring 
African markets.
The requirement extended beyond handling call volumes. Customer interactions needed to be 
managed consistently across languages, channels, products and customer types, while maintaining 
service levels, quality assurance and operational continuity.

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 62 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
ONE ENVIRONMENT FOR CUSTOMER ENGAGEMENT
MPC implemented an integrated multilingual contact centre combining VoIP, customised 
CRM integration, contact routing, quality assurance, automated reporting and structured 
escalation processes.
Customer interactions are monitored across customer type, language, communication channel, 
product, inbound and outbound activity, voice of the customer surveys and technical support 
requests. Business continuity capabilities support continuous service delivery.

--- Section D008 | [AR] physical page 62 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
IMPROVING SERVICE PERFORMANCE
Customer support without the geographic constraint
The model extends access to customer service and technical support across 11 African markets, 
while integrated quality and reporting processes provide the client with greater visibility over 
service performance.
Multiple ways to engage
Customers can engage across multiple channels and languages, allowing service and technical 
support to respond to different customer needs across markets.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote `* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology`** [D008, p. 56]: Attached to **"R4.1 billion*"** (MARKET SERVED). This is a **management-defined market-sizing methodology**, not an audited or third-party market figure. It changes the headline: the R4.1bn is **addressable market**, not iOCO revenue. Must be verified against Note 22 for actual People Solutions revenue to calculate implied market share. The methodology itself is not disclosed in this section — verification question raised (see Q167 below).

- **Footnote `* Management ambition`** [D008, p. 56]: Attached to **"10%*"** (MARKET SHARE AMBITION). This is **aspirational**, not achieved. The 10% ambition over FY2027–2029 implies ~R410m revenue at full ambition (10% × R4.1bn). Must NOT be treated as achieved share. Verification question raised (see Q168 below).

- **Footnote markers `[^Hi][^gh] [^Me][^dL][^ow]`** [D008, p. 56]: Attached to the MARKET OPPORTUNITY column header. **No footnote definitions are present in this capture.** This is now the **third consecutive segmental page** (D006 p. 43, D007 p. 47, D008 p. 56) carrying these undefined markers. They appear to be **layout artefacts** (superscript styling fragments from the PDF template), not true footnotes. However, this cannot be confirmed without image re-capture. **Do NOT fabricate definitions.** Verification question escalated (see Q141/Q156).

- **Footnote `* Completion rate calculated against learners whose interventions had concluded, excluding those still active (1 862 in FY2026)`** [D008, p. 59]: Attached to the regional completion-rate table. This is a **material qualification**: the 89.5% total completion rate is calculated on **1,862 completed learners**, excluding **1,862 still-active learners** (i.e., 50% of the 3,037 enrolled cohort is still active). The headline "96% learner completion" [D008, p. 57] is **inconsistent** with the 89.5% table figure — a **discrepancy** requiring verification (see Q169 below). The 96% may refer to a different metric (e.g., service levels) or a different cohort.

- **Qualification "Public sector 5% of division"** [D008, p. 56]: Materially lower than the 22% disclosed for Infrastructure Solutions (D006) and Forensics/Legal/HC (D007). Confirms public-sector concentration is **division-specific**, not group-uniform. Group-level public-sector weighting must be derived from Note 22 disaggregation (Q146/Q157).

- **Qualification "Recurring revenue 90% of base"** [D008, p. 56]: A **third distinct recurring metric** across divisions (D006: 10% recurring / 90% managed services; D007: 60% recurring+licensing / 85% opening base; D008: 90% recurring). Confirms **inconsistent recurring-revenue definitions by division**. Group-level recurring % from Note 22 (Q117) is now critical for forecasting.

- **Qualification "Renewal rates: L&D 90%; BPO 96%"** [D008, p. 56]: A **third and fourth renewal metric** across divisions (D007: 97% vs 95% discrepancy). Confirms renewal-rate definitions vary by division. Must be verified against Note 22 contract renewal/backlog disclosure (Q154).

- **Qualification "1 760 contractors placed"** [D008, p. 56]: Contractors are **not employees** — they are placed with clients. This affects headcount reconciliation (Q113/Q136) and employee-cost note (Q70). Must confirm whether contractor costs are in cost of sales or employee costs.

- **Qualification "4 100 learners"** [D008, p. 56]: Learners are **not employees** — they are training beneficiaries. Must NOT be included in headcount reconciliation.

- **Qualification "622 contact centre employees"** [D008, p. 56]: Contact-centre employees are a **distinct labour category** from permanent employees (144). Must confirm whether contact-centre labour is in cost of sales (direct labour) or employee costs (opex) — material for gross margin analysis (Q38).

- **Qualification "144 permanent employees"** [D008, p. 56]: Permanent headcount only. Combined with 622 contact-centre = 766 permanent/contact-centre. Must reconcile to employee-cost note (Q70).

- **Qualification "57 qualifications registered; most SETA qualifications extended; 10% of portfolio migrated"** [D008, p. 57]: **SETA-to-QCTO transition risk** — only 10% of portfolio migrated. This is a **regulatory execution risk** that could affect FY2027 revenue recognition and accreditation. Must check Note 39 subsequent events and Note 32 provisions for any regulatory exposure (Q170 below).

- **Qualification "AI disruption of seat-based BPO models and tutoring (Connect)"** [D008, p. 57]: **High risk** — AI is shrinking seat-based BPO. Growth must come from **platform-led and IP revenue** [D008, p. 56]. This is a **structural margin risk** for the BPO division. Must check Note 22 for BPO revenue mix and Note 24 for any restructuring/impairment (Q171 below).

- **Qualification "Client concentration in tutoring and talent"** [D008, p. 57]: **High risk** — concentration in tutoring and talent. Response: "New Client diversification; tighter debtor management." Must check Note 22 top-10 customer concentration and Note 38 ECL on concentrated debtors (Q112/Q32).

- **Qualification "Talent shortages and skills obsolescence in digital and emerging technology"** [D008, p. 57]: **Medium risk** — "limited host and absorption employers noted." Must check Note 24 for retention/SBP provisioning and employee-cost note for scarce-skill premiums (Q159/Q50).

- **Qualification "After two years of consolidation, People Solutions is positioned for growth in FY2027"** [D008, p. 57]: **Forward-looking claim** — implies FY2025 and FY2026 were consolidation years (likely revenue decline or flat). Must verify against Note 22 FY2026 vs FY2025 revenue for People Solutions (Q172 below).

- **Qualification "Proposed: outsourcing and reskilling demand is favourable, but AI is shrinking seat-based BPO; growth must come from platform-led and IP revenue"** [D008, p. 56]: **Mixed forward-looking claim** — favourable demand but structural AI headwind. Must verify platform/IP revenue quantification in Note 22 (Q171).

- **Qualification "Own scheduling and workforce tools"** [D008, p. 56]: **Own-IP claim** — must confirm capitalization in Note 2.5/Note 6 (Q95/Q160).

- **Qualification "3 037 learners enrolled across four regions"** [D008, p. 58]: **Operational KPI** — not revenue. Must confirm per-learner revenue model if disclosed (Q166).

- **Qualification "36.5% of learners placed were persons with disabilities. Of these learners, 57 were female and 44 male"** [D008, p. 58]: **Operational KPI** — 57 + 44 = 101 learners with disabilities. 36.5% of placed learners implies ~277 placed learners. Must confirm whether disability-inclusive programmes attract separate funding/revenue (Q173 below).

- **Qualification "Cape Town 225 learners / 74 completed / 78.7%; Gqeberha 1 583 / 946 / 92.0%; Johannesburg 402 / 295 / 91.6%; Pretoria 827 / 547 / 85.9%; Total 3 037 / 1 862 / 89.5%"** [D008, p. 59]: **Regional completion table** — arithmetic checks: 225+1,583+402+827 = 3,037 ✓; 74+946+295+547 = 1,862 ✓; 1,862/3,037 = 61.3% (not 89.5%). The 89.5% is calculated on **concluded interventions only** (1,862 completed ÷ ~2,081 concluded), excluding 1,862 still-active. **Material qualification** — the 89.5% is not the completion rate of the full cohort. Must verify the 96% headline against this table (Q169).

- **Qualification "1 862 learners successfully completed their qualifications"** [D008, p. 59]: **Operational KPI** — confirms 1,862 completed. Must confirm whether completion triggers revenue recognition (e.g., outcome-based funding) (Q173).

Must confirm workforce-model revenue (per-head vs per-store) in Note 22 (Q140).

Must confirm MPC revenue model (per-seat vs per-transaction) in Note 22 (Q140).

Must confirm Digital Talent revenue model (per-hour vs per-project) in Note 22 (Q140).

ADDRESSING A CASH FLOW CONSTRAINT FOR SMMES
SMMEs supplying goods and services to the public sector can face financial pressure when payment 
for completed work is delayed. The programme required a centralised mechanism through which 
businesses could raise, track and seek resolution of outstanding payment queries.
iOCO implemented the Public Sector SMME Payment Assistance Hotline for a public-sector 
small business support agency, providing businesses with a multilingual, omnichannel route to 
payment assistance.

SUPPORTING THE FLOW OF PAYMENTS TO SMALL BUSINESSES
The programme managed queries relating to approximately R320 million in outstanding public￾sector payments, with 94% of payment queries successfully closed.
This gave SMMEs a structured mechanism for navigating payment disputes while improving visibility 
and accountability across the payment-assistance process.
FROM RESOLUTION TO ECONOMIC PARTICIPATION
Timely payment matters to smaller suppliers because working capital supports their ability to 
continue operating and meet business obligations. The payment-assistance service provides a 
route for SMMEs to raise unresolved public-sector payment issues and seek resolution through 
a structured process.
CREATING A PATHWAY FROM OUTSTANDING PAYMENT TO 
BUSINESS CONTINUITY
By giving SMMEs a dedicated route to raise and resolve public-sector payment queries, the service 
supports greater visibility and accountability in the payment process; helping address a working￾CREATING A SINGLE ROUTE TO PAYMENT ASSISTANCE capital constraint faced by smaller suppliers.
The service combines a dedicated hotline, online query logging and request-a-callback functionality 
with payment negotiation support. A customised CRM, call recording, quality assurance and 
reporting provide visibility over queries and support SLA management.

RESPONDING TO GROWING DIGITAL DEMAND
As the client expanded its digital services, departments faced growing demand for citizen-facing 
applications, legacy-system modernisation and specialist technology skills.
EMBEDDING CAPABILITY WITHIN GOVERNMENT TEAMS
Since 2016, iOCO has provided technology professionals who work alongside personnel as 
integrated members of departmental delivery teams. Roles have included full-stack, front-end and 
back-end developers, scrum masters, project managers, DevOps engineers, database specialists, 
quality assurance testers and UX/UI designers. 
The model enables departments to scale development capacity according to project demand while 
retaining governance, architecture control and operational ownership within the entity. Working 
directly alongside the client’s teams also supports continuous knowledge transfer rather than 
positioning skills transfer only at the end of an engagement. 
BUILDING CAPABILITY ALONGSIDE GOVERNMENT TEAMS
Working alongside client teams increases delivery capacity while enabling iOCO specialists and 
government teams to work within shared delivery environments. Over the partnership, the model 
has supported application modernisation, integration and citizen-facing digital services across 
provincial government. 
PARTICIPATION THROUGH PUBLIC-SECTOR CAPABILITY

department.

devices even without network connectivity, synchronising it when connectivity returns. Dynamic 
forms reduce duplication, while simplified layouts and training support adoption across different 
levels of digital experience.

FY2026 SCALE
EXTENDING THE MODEL

social services.

The "R41 billion" SA software engineering market size is a market-sizing claim (source unstated) — treat as external market context, not company revenue.
- **"AI-native SDLC" / "Academy planned for FY2027" [D009, p. 64]**: Forward-looking capability investment (academy, AI-native SDLC) implies future cost build (training, tooling) in FY2027 — no rand quantification given. Flag for cost-side verification.
- **"Client renewal rate Year on year 90%" and "delivery with 10% shorter term projects" [D009, p. 64]**: A 90% renewal rate is a positive recurring-revenue quality signal, but "10% shorter term projects" implies **contract duration compression** — a potential revenue-recognition timing and working-capital (unbilled WIP) risk. No rand values attached.
- **"Application managed services -39%" [D009, p. 64]**: Ambiguous fragment — reads as a **39% decline (or a 39% mix figure) in application managed services**. This is a material anomaly given management's stated strategy to *grow* AMS and shift to recurring revenue. **Must be reconciled** — is this a revenue decline, a margin, or a mix percentage? Critical verification question (Q-D009-2).
- **"~500 SDLC engineers" / "500+ engineering professionals" [D009, pp. 64–65]**: Headcount baseline for technical labor cost modelling; no billable utilization rate disclosed.
- **"Average employment tenure is six years (twice SA market average)" [D009, p. 65]**: Retention quality signal; no cost quantification.
- **"30+ new engagements across six key industries" [D009, p. 65]**: Volume metric only; no contract value, no revenue contribution disclosed.
- **"R320 million in outstanding public-sector payments, 94% of payment queries closed" [D009, p. 66]**: This is a **client programme metric** (SMME hotline), NOT iOCO revenue. Do not confuse with company financials.
- **Industry mix [D009, p. 64]**: Financial services 73%, Telecommunications 7%, Public sector 6%, Automotive 5%, Retail 5%, Health 4% — sums to 100%. **Heavy concentration in financial services (73%)** — a client-concentration and sector-cyclicality risk for forecasting.

MOVING BEYOND RESOURCE-BASED SUPPORT
The provincial government’s SQL environment spans infrastructure and platform-based cloud 
deployments supporting applications across provincial departments.
Historically, database support relied on individual database administrators contracted on a resource￾for-time basis. As the environment became more complex, this created limited visibility across the 
SQL estate, dependency on individual resources and no consolidated approach to monitoring, 
reporting or capacity planning.
iOCO introduced a managed-service model combining operational support, estate-wide 
visibility, executive reporting and Azure PaaS management.

• Resource-based DBA support
• No consolidated SQL estate view
• Limited proactive monitoring
• Dependency on individual resources
• Limited capacity and cost visibility

--- Section D010 | [AR] physical page 72 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---

• Proactive operational checks

TURNING VISIBILITY INTO

consolidated view of the database estate,

and active projects, while daily monitoring of 
a provincial department’s Azure environment 
supports proactive management of backups, 
storage and capacity.
PLANNING AHEAD, NOT JUST 
RESPONDING

environment, iOCO introduced 90-day rolling 
capacity trend monitoring to identify future

operational issues.

The team also removed redundant backups

--- Section D010 | [AR] physical page 74 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
WHEN RECONCILIATION 
BECOMES A BOTTLENECK
The university’s Accounts Payable process 
requires supplier statements to be reconciled 
against transactions recorded in Oracle ERP 
before payments can proceed.
Previously, this involved manually comparing 
supplier statements with ERP records, 
recording discrepancies in spreadsheets 
and investigating exceptions individually. As 
volumes increased, the process required 
significant manual intervention and could delay 
the completion of payment runs.
1-2
DAYS EARLIER
AUTOMATING THE ROUTINE, 
FOCUSING PEOPLE ON 
EXCEPTIONS
Using Tungsten TotalAgility, iOCO automated 
the document-intensive stages of the 
reconciliation process.
Supplier emails and attachments are ingested 
automatically, statements are classified and 
relevant data extracted. The information is 
then matched against transactional data in 
Oracle ERP, with discrepancies identified for 
investigation. Once reviewed, reconciliation 
packs are routed for approval and archived in 
the content repository.
THE IMPACT
Automating the reconciliation process has 
enabled the university to complete payment 
runs one to two days earlier, while reducing 
the time Accounts Payable employees spend 
manually comparing records and capturing 
discrepancies.
Instead of reviewing every transaction 
manually, the process directs attention 
towards exceptions requiring investigation, 
enabling the Accounts Payable team to focus 
more of its capacity on resolving issues and 
higher-value activities

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology`** [D010, p. 70]: The R39bn "market served" figure is a **management-constructed market sizing**, not an external market research figure. This means the "+13.3% market share ambition" and "13% CAGR" are anchored to an internally defined denominator. **Forecast implication**: do not treat R39bn as an addressable-market TAM for revenue modelling; treat it as a directional management claim. Verify in D004 whether divisional revenue is reconciled to this market figure.

- **`* Management ambition`** [D010, p. 70]: The "+13.3%" and "Grow market share by 40% over three years" are explicitly labelled **ambition, not guidance**. **Forecast implication**: exclude from base-case revenue build; treat as upside scenario only.

- **`[^Hi][^gh][^Me][^dL][^ow]` marker cluster** [D010, p. 70]: Legend definitions are **not printed in the captured evidence**. The markers appear to encode risk ratings (High/Medium) and directional arrows (up/down) used elsewhere in the divisional pages, but the exact legend is missing from this capture. **Verification question raised** (see Q-D010-1 below).

- **Risk table ratings** [D010, p. 71]: "Leadership succession in a key business — High — New"; "Specialised talent scarcity and attrition; sales and pre-sales depth in security — High"; "Impression: platform modernisation; in-house e-signing alternatives; market saturation — Medium"; "Data and Analytics: maturing OEM portfolios; AI reshaping consulting — Medium". **Forecast implication**: two High-rated risks (succession, talent scarcity) are **unquantified** — no attrition %, no vacancy rate, no cost-to-fill disclosed. Verify in D004/D010 notes whether attrition and staff-cost inflation are quantified.

- **"Data and Analytics — a profitable year with healthy margins after a strategic reset"** [D010, p. 71]: "Strategic reset" is a **euphemism that typically masks restructuring or write-down charges**. No rand amount is disclosed in the captured pages. **Verification question raised** (Q-D010-2 below).

- **"Building security — strong revenue growth and a return to profit improvement"** [D010, p. 71]: "Return to profit improvement" implies the prior year was loss-making or margin-compressed. No prior-year comparative or rand figure printed. **Verification question raised** (Q-D010-3 below).

- **"62% of base on subscription and renewal revenue"** [D010, p. 70]: This is the only quantified recurring-revenue mix metric in the captured D010 pages. **Forecast implication**: 38% of the base is non-recurring (project/licence/one-off) — material lumpiness risk. Verify in D004 whether this 62% is revenue-weighted or contract-count-weighted.

- **"Renewal rate 95%"** [D010, p. 70]: High renewal rate supports recurring-revenue quality, but the **denominator (contract count vs revenue value) is not stated**. Verify in D004.

- **"Impression 100% contract renewal"** [D010, p. 70]: 100% is a suspiciously round figure — verify whether this is contract-count or revenue-weighted, and whether it excludes churned/non-renewed accounts.

- **"R2.6 million subscription and renewal revenue"** [D010, p. 70]: This appears to be a **sub-metric (likely Impression-specific or a per-unit metric)**, not divisional revenue. The unit basis is ambiguous — verify in D004 whether this is Impression ARR or a different metric.

- **"488 million signatures a year"** [D010, p. 70]: Volume metric with no revenue-per-signature disclosed. Verify in D004 whether signature volume is monetised per-transaction or bundled into subscription.

- **"6,600 readers across 602 workforce management sites"** [D010, p. 70]: Operational metric for the Workforce Management & Building Security proposition. No revenue per site/reader disclosed. Verify in D004.

- **"200+ customers; top 10 accounts renewed"** [D010, p. 70]: Top-10 concentration is **not quantified as % of revenue**. Verify in D004.

- **"9% of division"** [D010, p. 70, industries column]: Ambiguous — appears to attach to one industry vertical (likely public sector or healthcare). The exact referent is unclear from the captured layout. **Verification question raised** (Q-D010-4 below).

- **"One of three SAAA-accredited Advanced Electronic Signature providers in South Africa; WebTrust CA audit completed"** [D010, p. 71]: Regulatory moat claim — supports pricing power and defensibility. No financial quantification. Verify in D004 whether AES revenue is separately disclosed.

- **"22-instance SQL landscape documented"** [D010, p. 72]: Case-study operational metric — no contract value, term, or margin disclosed. **Forecast implication**: cannot be used to size managed-services revenue contribution.

- **"1–2 days earlier" payment runs** [D010, p. 74]: Client benefit metric — no iOCO revenue or margin impact disclosed.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **"R6.86 billion*" — footnote "* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology"** [D011, p. 77]. This is a **management-defined market-size estimate**, not an externally sourced TAM. It cannot be used as an independent revenue ceiling; it is a self-serving denominator for the 12% share ambition. Verification needed: the methodology itself (addressable vs served market, geography, product scope) is not printed — flag for D004 or any methodology note.

- **"12%*" — footnote "* Management ambition"** [D011, p. 77]. The 12% market-share target over 18 months is an **aspiration, not guidance**. It should not be modelled as a revenue forecast input; treat as qualitative.

- **`[^Hi][^gh] [^Me][^dL][^ow]` markers on MARKET OPPORTUNITY** [D011, p. 77]. **Footnote text is missing from this section capture** — no legend is printed on p. 77 or p. 78. Do not infer meaning. Create verification question (see Section 3).

- **`[^so][^ft][^wa][^re] [^OE][^M]` markers on PARTNERS AND IP** [D011, p. 77]. **Footnote text is missing from this section capture.** These appear to encode partner/OEM/IP attributes but the definitions are not printed. Do not reconstruct. Create verification question.

- **"Renewal rate over 12 months – 80%"** [D011, p. 77]. A qualification embedded in the CLIENTS column. It is a **12-month rolling renewal rate**, not a contract-value-weighted retention rate; the denominator (contract count vs value) is not stated. This is a key churn indicator for CASA recurring revenue — flag for reconciliation against D004 segmental recurring revenue.

- **"Public sector 25% of division"** [D011, p. 77]. Embedded in INDUSTRIES column. Confirms meaningful public-sector concentration — relevant to IFRS 9 ECL provisioning and payment-cycle/DSO risk. Rand amount and debtor aging not disclosed here.

- **"Estates supported 35+"** and **"43 certifications held"** [D011, p. 77]. Operational scale metrics, not financial. No revenue-per-estate or certification-cost disclosure.

- **Risk table** [D011, p. 78]: "Margin compression and foreign-exchange exposure — High" and "Scarce mainframe and technical skills — Medium (–)". The "vs FY2025" column shows **no directional change** for either risk (blank / "–"), implying both risks persisted at the same rating year-on-year. Margin compression + FX flagged High is a direct warning on CASA gross margin and technical labor cost — flag for D004 segmental margin.

BRINGING FRAGMENTED ASSET INFORMATION TOGETHER
The municipality manages more than R461 billion in infrastructure across 12 asset classes and every 
major directorate. Asset information and maintenance processes have historically been distributed 
across unit-specific systems, limiting a consistent city-wide view.
iOCO is implementing a Computerised Asset Management System (CAMS) using the municipality’s 
existing Oracle JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform. CAMS brings asset information, work orders 
and planned maintenance into a more integrated environment, connecting with finance and supply 
chain processes and operational systems used for geographic asset information, fault management 
and infrastructure monitoring.
CAMS forms Programme 9 of the municipality’s 14-programme Asset Management Improvement 
Plan and supports MFMA and National Treasury CIDMS requirements for compliant and auditable 
asset management. The capability uses the municipality’s existing Oracle JDE agreement, with R0 
additional JDE licence cost.
In May 2026 the Fleet Directorate successfully migrated off its legacy system onto 
JD Edwards CAMS. CAMS now maintains R2.8 billion in assets, has processed more than 
9 000 work orders to date, and is tracking a 93.3% vehicle availability rate.

--- Section D012 | [AR] physical page 83 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
BUILDING THE FOUNDATION FOR MORE RESILIENT 
INFRASTRUCTURE
CAMS is progressively creating a common view of municipal assets and maintenance activity. This 
strengthens the information foundation for lifecycle planning, asset-performance management and 
future capital investment; connecting stronger asset governance with the infrastructure on which 
municipal services depend.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`*` on "R29 billion+*" and "4%"** `[D012, p. 80]`: Footnote reads "* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology." — i.e., a **management-estimated addressable market**, not an independently verified figure. Same pattern as D011's "R6.86 billion*" (Q-D011-7). Methodology (addressable vs served, geography, product scope) is **not disclosed here** — must be verified in D004 or a methodology note.
- **`*` on "4% of market share"** `[D012, p. 80]`: Second footnote reads "* Management ambition." — so the "4% of market share within three years" and "Partner rank #1 for all strategic OEMs" are **aspirational targets, not achieved metrics**. Do not treat as baseline.
- **Bracketed markers `[^Hi][^gh]`, `[^Me][^dL][^ow]`, `[^In][^fo][^r]`, `[^Sy][^sp][^ro]`** `[D012, p. 80]`: **Footnote/legend text is missing from this section capture.** Based on the p. 81 RISKS table structure (Rating: High/Medium; vs FY2025: –), the first pair likely = risk rating + direction; the second pair (In/fo/r, Sy/sp/ro) likely = partner/IP descriptors (e.g., "Infor", "SYSPRO"). **Do not fabricate** — flag as verification question.
- **"Astraia acquired" / "Astraia acquisition completed and integrated post year-end"** `[D012, p. 80–81]`: Critical qualification — the acquisition is **post-year-end**, so FY2026 financials will **not** include Astraia revenue/EBITDA. Any FY2027 forecast must add Astraia as an inorganic step-up. Purchase consideration, goodwill, intangibles, and contingent consideration must be checked in the D010 business-combinations note (Q8).
- **"SYSPRO moving to subscription licensing"** `[D012, p. 80]`: Structural revenue-mix shift — near-term revenue recognition timing change (upfront licence → ratable subscription), affecting deferred revenue (contract liabilities) build and cash collection profile. Must be verified in D004/D010 revenue-recognition note.
- **"R0 additional JDE licence cost"** `[D012, p. 83]`: Case-study qualification — CAMS delivered on existing Oracle JDE agreement, so **no incremental licence resale revenue**; revenue is services/implementation only (lower-margin mix implication). Verify contract value/margin if disclosed.
- **"93.3% vehicle availability", "9 000 work orders", "R2.8 billion in assets"** `[D012, p. 83]`: Operational KPIs, **not financial** — no revenue or margin attached. Do not capitalise into forecast without contract value.

MOVING BEYOND FRAGMENTED BACKUP POWER
The client’s retail sites relied on multiple small, standalone UPS units protecting individual pieces of 
automation equipment. These units were not centrally monitored or standardised, creating multiple 
points of failure and a reactive maintenance environment.
Against a backdrop of severe load shedding, failure of backup power could take point of sale (POS) 
terminals, forecourt automation and back-office systems offline, interrupting trading and 
fuel transactions.
Compu-Power was appointed to implement a standardised, centralised UPS architecture across 
the retail network, replacing multiple individual units. Implementing a dedicated automation 
DB separation framework that isolates critical forecourt and POS equipment onto dedicated 
UPS sub-boards, eliminating overload trips caused by non-critical utility appliances.
LESS HARDWARE, GREATER VISIBILITY
What changed at site level when individual units were replaced by a centralised design

--- Section D013 | [AR] physical page 86 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
PROTECTING THE SYSTEMS BEHIND EVERY TRANSACTION
The centralised UPS environment protects critical forecourt infrastructure including POS terminals, 
automation systems and back-office networks, helping sites maintain essential digital functionality 
during power interruptions.
Each UPS is connected to the client’s network with SNMP-enabled telemetry, providing remote 
visibility of power status, battery health and fault alerts.
By FY2026 year end, 35 sites had been completed, protecting 219 POS terminals/forecourt 
systems and providing a minimum of on average two hours of backup capability per site

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`*` on "R4.2 billion*" and "growth*"** [D013, p. 84]: The asterisk resolves only to "* Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology" and "* Management ambition." **No methodology, source, base year, or currency basis is printed.** The R4.2bn "market served" figure cannot be reconciled to CIE revenue without the methodology — flag for D004 segmental revenue cross-check.

- **`[^Hi][^gh] [^Me][^dL][^ow]` markers** [D013, p. 84]: **Footnote text is missing from this section capture.** These appear to be risk-rating/direction superscripts (consistent with the p. 85 RISKS table "High / Medium" + "vs FY2025" columns), but the legend is not printed. Do not infer definitions.

- **"Forward load up strongly +56% year on year"** [D013, p. 84]: A forward-load (order book / pipeline) metric with **no rand value, no definition of "forward load," and no prior-year base disclosed**. This is a leading indicator for FY2027 revenue but is unquantified — verification question required.

- **"Revenue −2%"** [D013, p. 85, RISKS table]: The only hard revenue-direction datapoint in this section — CIE revenue **declined 2%** in FY2026, attributed to slow SA funding/procurement. This must be reconciled to the D004 segmental revenue line.

- **"Attrition 5%"** [D013, p. 85]: Division-level attrition only; no denominator (technical core vs total headcount) stated.

- **"309 people, 81% in the technical core"** [D013, p. 84]: Implies ~250 technical staff; **no billable utilisation %, no contractor vs permanent split, no technical labour cost %** disclosed.

- **"4 x own IP" / "Own IP: ecWIN, EI Enterprise, i-RAMS, OTMS: XaaS IOC"** [D013, p. 84]: Own-IP software is named but **no revenue, margin, or capitalisation disclosure** — relevant to IAS 38 capitalised development and recurring revenue quality.

- **"XaaS" / "recurring OT managed services"** [D013, pp. 84–85]: Recurring revenue is referenced qualitatively and as an FY2027 outlook metric ("XaaS renewal rate and new logos") but **no rand amount or ARR % is disclosed** — critical gap for recurring-mix forecasting.

- **"Trading conditions in South Africa have improved since year end"** [D013, p. 85]: Forward-looking qualification with no quantification — flag for D004/D003 management commentary cross-check.

- **Compu-Power case study** [D013, p. 86]: "35 sites completed, 219 POS terminals/forecourt systems, minimum ~2 hours backup per site" — **no contract value, term, or margin disclosed**; likely lumpy project revenue (UPS hardware + integration), not recurring.

- **"R450 billion* +R1 billion*" and "*Calculated according to iOCO market sizing methodology"** [D014, p. 92]: The market-served figure is management-estimated, not independently sourced. The "+R1 billion*" appears to be a market-share-gain ambition (revenue by FY2030), also asterisked to the same undefined methodology. Neither is auditable from this section; the methodology definition must be located (likely D004 or a group overview note). This is a soft, non-financial claim — do not use in the forecast model.
- **"MARKET OPPORTUNITY [^Hi][^gh] [^Me][^dL][^ow]"** [p. 92]: Footnote markers present, **footnote text is missing from this section capture**. Cannot be interpreted; verification question raised.

It confirms material customer concentration (consistent with the "High" risk rating on p. 93: "Customer concentration and contract retention... Materialised as contracts reached term; multi-year contracts partially replaced"). Implication: revenue is lumpy at contract-renewal boundaries; forecast should model renewal-cliff risk. - **"Renewal rate 92%"** [p. 92]: No denominator or rand amount. Cannot compute recurring revenue base from this alone.
